78.title: Janmashtami: the night Krishna was born
78.hook: a prison at midnight, a river that parts, and a baby carried across it to safety
78.carry: the avatar comes in the darkest hour
78.tomorrow: Ganesh Chaturthi: the moon that laughed
78.howItsDone: On Janmashtami many Hindus fast until midnight, sing devotional songs, and at the hour of Krishna's birth ring bells and rock a small cradle holding an image of baby Krishna; in Maharashtra the next day, teams form human pyramids to break a pot of curds hung high, as Krishna the butter thief would.

screen: `DAY SEVENTY-EIGHT.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: the driver. Krishna chose to hold the reins for Arjuna, and the stories camp closed. Today, the driver's first night.
screen: `YOU KNOW THESE PEOPLE NOW.`

segments.voice: A prison cell in the city of Mathura. Midnight, a storm outside. A mother, Devaki, and a father, Vasudeva, in chains. Her brother, the tyrant king Kamsa, was told at her wedding that her eighth child would kill him. So he locked them up and took every baby they had. Now the eighth is coming. Last time, Krishna was a grown man holding a chariot's reins; tonight's festival goes back to the very start. And the whole night is one question: can a newborn be carried out of a locked prison, across a flooding river, before morning?
screen: `A PRISON AT MIDNIGHT.` → `KAMSA FEARS THE EIGHTH CHILD.` → `CAN A BABY GET OUT BY MORNING?`

segments.voice: The Bhagavata Purana tells it like this. At midnight, the baby is born. The guards fall into a deep sleep. The chains fall from Vasudeva's wrists. The prison doors swing open on their own. Vasudeva puts his newborn son in a basket on his head and walks out into the storm, to the river Yamuna, in flood. And the river, in the story, lets him through; in a popular telling, the water rises to touch the baby's feet, then parts. The great serpent Shesha rises behind him and spreads his many hoods over the basket like an umbrella against the rain. On the far side, in the village of Gokul, the cowherd's wife Yashoda has just given birth to a daughter. Vasudeva quietly swaps the babies and walks back to his cell. In the morning Kamsa comes for the child, and the baby girl slips from his hands, rises into the sky as a goddess, and tells him: the one you fear is already born, somewhere else. That's Janmashtami: janma, birth, and ashtami, the eighth day of the moon's dark half, when tradition says he was born. Households that keep the festival fast all day and stay up until midnight, singing, and at the hour of the birth they ring bells and rock a tiny cradle. This is the Hindu teaching of the avatar: God coming down into the world. In the Gita, Krishna says he comes, age after age, whenever goodness declines. And look where he arrives: not a palace, a prison cell, at the darkest hour. Many devotees read the midnight vigil that way: God comes into the dark, not after it.

segments.voice: Dim the lights or close your eyes. If you pray, ring a bell once, or say softly Jai Shri Krishna, the way families do at midnight, and picture a tiny cradle rocking. If you don't pray, sit in the dark with something good you're still waiting for. Let the waiting be here, the way the family waited in the cell. Then picture one small light, the door opening a crack.

79.title: Ganesh Chaturthi: the moon that laughed
79.hook: the moon laughs at Ganesha's fall, and the clay goes back to the water
79.carry: god has a form, and is beyond it
79.tomorrow: Navaratri: nine nights of the Goddess
79.howItsDone: For Ganesh Chaturthi, Hindu families and neighborhoods install clay images of Ganesha at home or in public pandals, worship him with lamps, flowers, durva grass and modaks for one and a half to ten days, then immerse the image in water in a joyful procession; many avoid looking at the moon on the festival night, and many now choose unpainted clay. The great public festivals grew from Pune in the 1890s, with Bal Gangadhar Tilak.

screen: `DAY SEVENTY-NINE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: Janmashtami, a baby carried out of a prison through a flood at midnight. The avatar comes in the darkest hour.
screen: `THE AVATAR COMES IN THE DARKEST HOUR.`

segments.voice: Ganesh Chaturthi night, late summer. The drums have finally gone quiet. Your family's clay Ganesha is home on a little throne, with lamps, flowers and a plate of modaks, the sweet dumplings he loves. You step outside for air, and an aunt grabs your arm. Don't look up. Not tonight. Don't look at the moon. It sounds like a superstition. It's really the end of a story: a god who fell off his ride, and the one who laughed at him.
screen: `THE CLAY GANESHA IS HOME.` → `DON'T LOOK AT THE MOON.` → `WHO LAUGHED AT GANESHA?`

segments.voice: Here's the story as families tell it. It's Ganesha's birthday, and everyone has been feeding him modaks. Belly full, he rides home at night on his mouse. A snake slides across the path, the mouse panics, Ganesha tumbles off, and the sweets spill everywhere. He gets up, gathers them, and ties the snake around his middle as a belt. And up in the sky the moon, proud of his own beauty, laughs at the round god in the dust. Ganesha curses him: no one will want to look at you. The moon goes dark and begs, the gods plead, and Ganesha softens it: only on this one night, whoever looks at the moon will be wrongly blamed for something. The tellings say even Krishna glimpsed the moon that night and was accused of stealing a famous jewel, the Syamantaka, and had to clear his own name. So on Ganesh Chaturthi, many families keep their eyes off the moon. Now the teaching. Many teachers read the story this way: the moon laughed at a shape, the elephant head, the belly, the snake belt. He saw only the form. Hinduism has two words for this. Saguna: God with form and qualities, a face you can see, feed and love. Nirguna: God beyond every form. Many Hindus hold both, and the festival acts it out. For days, families love Ganesha in clay, the saguna way, with lamps and modaks. Then they carry him to the water and let the clay go, because he was never only the clay. The crowds shout Ganpati Bappa Morya, and in Marathi, come back soon next year. The form goes. The god doesn't. It's why a Hindu home can hold many pictures of God, and still say God is one, beyond them all.
screen: `THE MOUSE, THE SNAKE, THE SPILLED SWEETS.` · `THE MOON LAUGHS.` · `THE MOON SAW ONLY A SHAPE.` · `SAGUNA AND NIRGUNA.` · then, large: `GOD HAS A FORM, AND IS BEYOND IT.`

segments.voice: If you pray, look at a picture or murti of Ganesha, or any face of God you love, for one slow minute: the eyes, the hands, the small details. Say his name, or Om Gam Ganapataye Namah. Then close your eyes, let the picture fade, and stay with what's still there. If you don't pray, do it with a photo of someone you love. The picture goes. The love stays.

80.title: Navaratri: nine nights of the Goddess
80.hook: Durga meets the buffalo demon; nine nights of dancing, and on the tenth day the good wins
80.carry: durga: the power of every god, as mother
80.howItsDone: During Navaratri, Hindus honor the Goddess over nine nights in regional ways: garba and dandiya dancing in Gujarat, Durga Puja in Bengal, displays of dolls (golu) in the south, fasting and recitation of the Devi Mahatmya in many homes; the tenth day, Vijayadashami or Dussehra, celebrates the victory of good.

screen: `DAY EIGHTY.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: Ganesh Chaturthi, a moon that laughed and a clay god given back to the water. God has a form, and is beyond it.
screen: `GOD HAS A FORM, AND IS BEYOND IT.`

segments.voice: Eleven at night in Gujarat, and an open ground is packed. People in mirrored skirts and embroidered jackets move in huge circles, clapping, spinning, sticks clicking in rhythm. They'll be back tomorrow night, and the night after: nine nights in a row. Far to the east, in Bengal, neighborhoods build glittering temporary halls for a ten-armed goddess on a lion. In the south, families set out steps of dolls. Different places, different customs, the same nine nights. And at the center of many of them, one story: a demon nobody could defeat, and the Goddess who did.
screen: `NINE NIGHTS OF DANCING.` → `A TEN-ARMED GODDESS ON A LION.` → `A DEMON NOBODY COULD DEFEAT.`

segments.voice: The story comes from the Devi Mahatmya, the Glory of the Goddess, a Sanskrit text recited in homes and temples during these nights. Mahishasura, a demon who is part buffalo, grows so powerful that he drives the gods out of heaven. The gods are so furious that their anger bursts out of them as light, and the light of every god flows together into one blazing form: a woman. The Goddess. Each god hands her a weapon: Shiva's trident, Vishnu's discus, and a lion to ride. People call her Durga, the one who is hard to reach, hard to defeat. She rides out laughing. Mahishasura keeps changing shape to escape her: a buffalo, a lion, a warrior with a sword, an elephant, a buffalo again. She meets every form, and as he struggles half out of the buffalo's body, she ends it. That's why images of Durga so often show her spear in a buffalo. Now the teaching. She isn't the gods' helper. She is all their power in one: Shakti, God as Mother, the power behind everything that moves. What no single god could do, she does. Many teachers read the buffalo as the stubborn, dull part of us that keeps changing disguise, and these nights as asking the Mother to meet it. Navaratri: nava, nine, and ratri, night. Some honor nine forms of the Goddess, one each night. Some dance the garba for her. The tenth day, Vijayadashami, is the day of victory; in much of north India it's also Dussehra, for Rama's victory over Ravana.
screen: `THE GODS' LIGHT BECOMES THE GODDESS.` · `DURGA MEETS EVERY FORM HE TAKES.` · `SHAKTI: GOD AS MOTHER, THE POWER OF ALL.` · `NAVA + RATRI: NINE NIGHTS.` · then, large: `DURGA: THE POWER OF EVERY GOD, AS MOTHER.`

segments.voice: Many families light a lamp for the Goddess on each of these nights. If you pray, light one, or picture one, and say Jai Mata Di, victory to the Mother, or simply, Ma. Then name one thing that keeps changing shape on you: the urge to snap, the voice that says you're not enough. Ask for her strength to meet it, just tonight. If you don't pray, name it, and decide: not tonight.
Navaratri. Nava, nine; ratri, night. Nine nights of the Goddess, and on the tenth day, victory.

81.title: Diwali: from darkness to light
81.hook: Krishna opens a demon king's prison, and the lamps go on before dawn
81.carry: from darkness, lead me to light
81.howItsDone: For Diwali, Hindu families clean and decorate their homes, draw rangoli patterns at the door, light rows of clay lamps, worship Lakshmi on the new-moon night, share sweets, and visit relatives; customs and the stories told vary by region over the festival's five days.

screen: `DAY EIGHTY-ONE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: Navaratri, nine nights of the Goddess. Durga: the power of every god, as mother.
screen: `DURGA: THE POWER OF EVERY GOD, AS MOTHER.`

segments.voice: Five in the morning, still pitch dark, in a house in south India. A grandmother is rubbing warm oil into a sleepy child's hair before a bath. Firecrackers are already popping down the street, and a pattern of colored powder waits at the door. Far to the north, people are waiting for tonight's lamps for Rama, the story you already know. Here, the lamps go on before sunrise, for a different story: Krishna, and a demon king who kept thousands of people locked in the dark.
screen: `FIVE A.M., WARM OIL, A BATH.` → `IN THE NORTH, LAMPS FOR RAMA.` → `A KING WHO LOCKED PEOPLE IN THE DARK.`

segments.voice: The Bhagavata Purana tells it. A demon king named Narakasura has grown so strong that he's stolen the earrings of Aditi, the mother of the gods, and locked away more than sixteen thousand princesses in his fortress. Krishna flies there on Garuda, the great eagle, with his queen Satyabhama beside him. He breaks through walls of fire and water, defeats Naraka's five-headed guard, Mura, and then Naraka himself. In many southern tellings, it's Satyabhama who strikes the final blow. Then the prison is thrown open, and sixteen thousand women walk out into the light. A popular telling adds that Naraka, dying, asked to be remembered with lamps. So on Naraka Chaturdashi, many families wake before dawn, bathe with oil, and light lamps while it's still dark. In the north, the lamps are for Rama coming home. On the main night, the new moon, many families welcome Lakshmi, the goddess of fortune and well-being, with open doors. Jains and Sikhs light lamps in this season too, for their own stories. Different stories, the same lamps. Now the teaching under all of them. An old prayer from the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad, still chanted today, asks: lead me from the unreal to the real, from darkness to light, from death to what doesn't die. The Upanishad itself explains it: the darkness is death; the light is what doesn't die. Many teachers also hear it as a prayer to wake from not-knowing into what's real. Every Diwali lamp is that prayer, made of clay and oil. It's why a family lights clay lamps in a house full of electric light. The lamp isn't for seeing the room. It's asking to see what's real.
screen: `NARAKASURA LOCKS THEM AWAY.` · `KRISHNA AND SATYABHAMA OPEN THE PRISON.` · `LAMPS BEFORE DAWN.` · `TAMASO MA JYOTIR GAMAYA.` · then, large: `FROM DARKNESS, LEAD ME TO LIGHT.`

segments.voice: Light one light if you can: a diya, a candle, even a phone screen turned toward you. If you pray, say the old line slowly, three times: tamaso ma jyotir gamaya, from darkness lead me to light. Then think of one place in your life where you can't see yet: a decision, a worry, a question about who you really are. Don't fix it. Just hold the light up to it, and ask to see. If you don't pray, simply ask the question, and sit with the flame.
Diwali. The row of lamps: many stories, one prayer, lit on the darkest night of the month.

segments.voice: Your line: from darkness, lead me to light. Every lamp says it. Day eighty-one, done.

screen: `DAY EIGHTY-TWO.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: Diwali, a prison thrown open and lamps before dawn. From darkness, lead me to light.
screen: `FROM DARKNESS, LEAD ME TO LIGHT.`

segments.voice: A street in north India, on a spring morning. Somebody's uncle is purple. A grandmother is laughing with green powder in her hair. A stranger you've never met walks up, says happy Holi, and smears pink on your cheek, and you do the same back. Water balloons from a balcony. Drums from somewhere. By noon you can't tell the banker from the delivery driver, or the neighbor you haven't spoken to in a year from your own cousin. Everyone is the same muddy, glorious color. But the night before, there was a fire, and the fire is where the story is.
screen: `A STRANGER SMEARS PINK ON YOUR CHEEK.` → `NOBODY CAN TELL WHO IS WHO.` → `BUT FIRST, A FIRE.`

segments.voice: The story is about a boy named Prahlad. His father, Hiranyakashipu, is a demon king with a boon that makes him nearly impossible to kill, and he decides that makes him God. Everyone in the kingdom must worship him. His own son won't. Prahlad keeps saying the name of Vishnu. The Bhagavata Purana tells how his father tries everything: snakes, elephants, a cliff, poison. The boy survives each one. Then comes the part the festival remembers. The king's sister, Holika, is said to be protected from fire. She takes Prahlad on her lap and sits down in a blazing pyre. And the fire turns. Holika burns. The boy walks out unharmed, still saying the name. An honest note: the Bhagavata tells Prahlad's story and ends it with Narasimha; the Holika scene comes from later tellings and the festival itself. Either way, the heart is the same, and it's one of Hinduism's most loved practices: the Name. Repeating God's name, called japa, or singing it together, kirtan. Prahlad had no army, only the name, and in the story it was enough. So on the full-moon night of Phalguna, at the end of winter, people light bonfires called Holika Dahan, and many walk around them, remembering a fire that couldn't hold a child. The next morning, the colors. People say it with a grin: bura na mano, Holi hai. Don't be offended, it's Holi. For one day the lines between people get smudged on purpose, and old quarrels are supposed to end. Holi has other stories too, and i'll come back for them.

83.title: Maha Shivaratri: the great night of Shiva
83.hook: a night kept awake, water poured over the lingam, Om Namah Shivaya until dawn
83.carry: bholenath: shiva is pleased by the smallest offering
83.tomorrow: Raksha Bandhan: the thread of protection
83.howItsDone: On Maha Shivaratri many Hindus fast, visit Shiva temples, pour water, milk or honey over the Shiva lingam with bilva leaves, and keep a vigil through the night chanting Om Namah Shivaya until dawn.

screen: `DAY EIGHTY-THREE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: Holi, a boy in a fire and colors in the morning. The name of god outlasts the fire.
screen: `THE NAME OF GOD OUTLASTS THE FIRE.`

segments.voice: This festival happens in the dark. Once a year, on the fourteenth night of the waning moon, just before the new moon, in late winter, Shiva temples stay open all night. The lines go around the block. People carry small brass pots of water and milk. They've been fasting since morning, and they're not going to bed. Inside, the sound doesn't stop: a bell, a chant, Om Namah Shivaya, again and again, until the sky starts to go gray. It's called Maha Shivaratri, the great night of Shiva. And one story people tell about it is about a man who stayed awake by accident.
screen: `A FESTIVAL IN THE DARK.` → `TEMPLES OPEN ALL NIGHT.` → `A MAN AWAKE BY ACCIDENT.`

segments.voice: The story comes from the Shiva Purana. A hunter goes into the forest, catches nothing all day, and night falls. Afraid of wild animals, he climbs a tree to wait for morning. It happens to be a bilva tree, whose three-part leaves are sacred to Shiva. And at its foot, hidden in the dark, is a Shiva lingam, the smooth rounded stone that stands for Shiva in temples. The hunter has no idea. All night, to stay awake and keep watch, he fidgets, and leaves drop from the branches onto the stone below. Water spills from his flask onto it. He hasn't eaten. He doesn't sleep. By dawn, without meaning to, he has done everything this night asks: fasted, kept awake, offered water and bilva leaves to Shiva. In the tellings, when deer come by he lets them go, and his heart changes. And Shiva frees him. His intention wasn't holy. He was just scared and stuck in a tree. That's why Shiva is called Bholenath, the simple-hearted lord, and Ashutosh, the one quickly pleased. He doesn't ask for gold. A pot of water, a leaf, a night awake. So that's what people do on Shivaratri; ratri means night. They fast, keep a vigil through the night's four watches, and pour water, milk or honey over the lingam, an offering called abhisheka, then lay bilva leaves on top. Different families remember different reasons for the night. Some say it's Shiva's wedding to Parvati, some say his dance; i'll come back to those.
screen: `A HUNTER UP A TREE.` · `LEAVES FALL ON A HIDDEN STONE.` · `BHOLENATH: QUICKLY PLEASED.` · `FAST, KEEP WATCH, POUR WATER.` · then, large: `SHIVA IS PLEASED BY THE SMALLEST OFFERING.`

segments.voice: Sit, and lower your eyes. If you pray, say Om Namah Shivaya, slowly, once with each breath out. If you have a little water nearby, pour a few drops onto a plant or the earth, the simplest offering there is. If you don't pray, just watch your breath. When something in you says that's enough, take three more. Like the hunter on his branch: not holy, just staying.
Shivaratri. The night of Shiva. Once a year, the great one, kept awake until dawn.

84.title: Raksha Bandhan: the thread of protection
84.hook: a sister ties a thread on her brother's wrist, and he promises to look after her
84.carry: raksha: protecting each other is dharma
84.howItsDone: On the full moon of Shravana, sisters tie a rakhi on their brothers' wrists with a lamp, a forehead mark and sweets, and brothers give a gift and a promise of protection; many families now tie it between sisters, cousins and close friends too.

screen: `DAY EIGHTY-FOUR.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: Shivaratri, a hunter up a tree, awake all night. Bholenath: Shiva is pleased by the smallest offering. Today, the smallest festival object there is: a thread.
screen: `SHIVA IS PLEASED BY THE SMALLEST OFFERING.`

segments.voice: A summer morning, the full moon of the month of Shravana. In homes across India and far beyond, a sister sets out a small plate: a little lamp, a pinch of red powder, a few sweets, and a thread. Sometimes it's a plain red and gold string. Sometimes it's a glittering thing with a plastic cartoon on it, because her brother is six. She marks his forehead, circles the lamp in front of his face, ties the thread around his wrist, and pops a sweet in his mouth. He gives her a gift, and a promise: I'll look after you. Brothers on other continents get their threads in the mail.
screen: `A PLATE, A LAMP, A THREAD.` → `TIED AROUND HIS WRIST.` → `I'LL LOOK AFTER YOU.`

segments.voice: Raksha means protection. Bandhan means a tie, a bond. Raksha Bandhan: the tie of protection. The thread itself is called a rakhi. It's small enough to snap with two fingers, yet people keep it on for days, because of what it holds. The best-known story behind it isn't really in the old texts, and it's worth saying so. People tell that Krishna once cut his finger, and Draupadi, without a second thought, tore a strip from the edge of her sari and tied it around the wound. Krishna was moved, and promised to protect her. Years later, in the Mahabharata, Draupadi is dragged into a hall full of men and humiliated, and her sari is pulled. And the cloth doesn't end. It keeps coming, and she's covered. The Mahabharata tells the endless cloth; the torn strip and the promise are how many families tell why. A strip of cloth for a strip of cloth. Care offered first, and the promise answers it. Here's the teaching under the thread. Raksha, protection, is dharma: a duty, not a favor. And in the telling families love, the one who keeps the promise is God himself; when Draupadi had no one, Krishna covered her. In many families the thread now goes both ways: sisters, cousins, close friends. That's the week: a birth at midnight, a moon that laughed, nine nights of the Goddess, lamps against the dark, a boy in a fire, a night awake, and now a thread.
screen: `RAKSHA — PROTECTION. BANDHAN — A TIE.` · `A STRIP OF CLOTH FOR A STRIP OF CLOTH.` · `CARE FIRST, THEN THE PROMISE.` · `PROTECTING IS DHARMA.` · then, large: `RAKSHA: PROTECTING EACH OTHER IS DHARMA.`

segments.voice: Let a face come: a sibling, a child, a parent getting older, a friend having a rough year. Picture tying a thread around their wrist, slowly, the way it's done. If you pray, ask God to protect them, the way a rakhi asks. Then say it inside, in your own words: I've got you. And think of one small way to keep that promise this week.
Rakhi. The thread tied on Raksha Bandhan, the tie of protection. Small enough to snap, strong enough to hold a promise.
